title: Ezekiel Chapter 29 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Ezekiel chapter 29 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Ezekiel Chapter 29 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Ezekiel Chapter 29.

questions.question: In Ezekiel 29, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: The word of the LORD came unto me
I will put hooks in thy jaws
I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness
questions.correctAnswer: The word of the LORD came unto me
questions.explanation: This is the first event mentioned in the chapter, found in Ezekiel 29:1.

questions.question: To whom did the word of the LORD come in Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: The text states that the word of the LORD came unto me, which refers to Ezekiel himself, as stated in Ezekiel 29:1.

questions.question: What is Pharaoh king of Egypt compared to in Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:3 refers to Pharaoh as 'the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers.'

questions.question: What will God put in Pharaoh's jaws according to Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:4 mentions that God will put 'hooks in thy jaws.'

questions.question: What will happen to the fish of Pharaoh's rivers according to Ezekiel 29?
options: They shall stick unto thy scales
They will be thrown into the wilderness
questions.correctAnswer: They shall stick unto thy scales
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:4 states that 'all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales.'

questions.question: What does God say He will leave Pharaoh and the fish of his rivers in Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:5 says, 'And I will leave thee thrown into the wilderness.'

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29, what will happen to Pharaoh's body?
options: It will be thrown into the wilderness
It will float in the river
questions.correctAnswer: It will be thrown into the wilderness
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:5 states that Pharaoh 'shall fall upon the open fields; thou shalt not be brought together, nor gathered.'

questions.question: What will all the inhabitants of Egypt know according to Ezekiel 29?
options: That they should fear the beasts
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:6 states, 'And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD.'

questions.question: What did the Egyptians provide to the house of Israel according to Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:6 indicates that they have been a 'staff of reed to the house of Israel.'

questions.question: What happened when the house of Israel leaned upon Pharaoh according to Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:7 states, 'thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder.'

questions.question: What did Pharaoh do when they took hold of him by the hand according to Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:7 states, 'thou didst break, and rend all their shoulder.'

questions.question: The inhabitants of Egypt will know that I am the LORD. Is this statement true?
questions.explanation: This is directly stated in Ezekiel 29:6.

questions.question: Pharaoh king of Egypt is referred to as a dragon in Ezekiel 29. Is this statement true?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:3 describes Pharaoh as 'the great dragon.'

questions.question: The fish of the rivers will swim away according to Ezekiel 29. Is this statement true?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:4 states that the fish shall stick unto Pharaoh's scales, not swim away.

questions.question: The beasts of the field will not eat Pharaoh according to Ezekiel 29. Is this statement true?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:5 mentions that Pharaoh has been given for meat to the beasts of the field.

medium.title: Ezekiel Chapter 29 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Ezekiel Chapter 29 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What will happen to man and beast in Egypt according to Ezekiel 29:8?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:8 states, 'Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will bring a sword upon thee, and cut off man and beast out of thee.' This indicates that both man and beast will be removed from Egypt.

questions.question: What does Ezekiel 29:9 promise will happen if Pharaoh does not recognize the LORD?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:9 states, 'And the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste; and they shall know that I am the LORD.' This indicates that if Pharaoh does not acknowledge God, the land will face desolation.

questions.question: What will happen to the rivers of Egypt according to Ezekiel 29:10?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:10 states, 'Behold, therefore I am against thee, and against thy rivers.' This signifies that God is opposing Pharaoh and his rivers.

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29:12, how long will Egypt be desolate?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:12 states, 'her cities among the cities that are laid waste shall be desolate forty years.' This indicates a specific duration of desolation.

questions.question: What will happen to the Egyptians according to Ezekiel 29:13?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:13 states, 'Yet thus saith the Lord GOD; At the end of forty years will I gather the Egyptians from the people whither they were scattered.' This indicates a future restoration.

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29:14, where will the Egyptians return to?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:14 states, 'I will bring again the captivity of Egypt, and will cause them to return into the land of Pathros.' This specifies the location of their return.

questions.question: How does Ezekiel 29:7 describe the Egyptians' effect on Israel?
options: They were like a staff of reed
They were a source of prosperity
questions.correctAnswer: They were like a staff of reed
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:6 states, 'because they have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel.' This metaphor indicates their weakness and unreliability.

questions.question: What does Ezekiel 29:4 reveal about Pharaoh's reliance on his rivers?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:3 mentions Pharaoh saying, 'My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself.' This reveals his arrogance and pride in his own power, which is seen as foolishness.

questions.question: What will be the state of the land of Egypt according to Ezekiel 29:9?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:9 states, 'And the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste.' This directly indicates the consequence of not acknowledging God.

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29:11, what will not pass through Egypt for forty years?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:11 states, 'No foot of man shall pass through it, nor foot of beast shall pass through it.' This shows the complete desolation of the land.

questions.question: What does the desolation of Egypt symbolize for the Israelites according to Ezekiel 29?
questions.explanation: The desolation of Egypt serves as a clear sign of judgment from God, emphasizing His authority and the consequences of disobedience.

questions.question: The Egyptians will be scattered among the nations according to Ezekiel 29:12. What does this indicate about God's sovereignty?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:12 indicates God's sovereign control over the nations as He scatters the Egyptians, showcasing His power over all peoples.

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29:8, God will bring a sword upon Egypt. What does this imply about God's view of sin?
questions.explanation: The implication is that God takes sin seriously and will enact judgment as stated in Ezekiel 29:8, highlighting His holiness.

questions.question: Ezekiel 29:5 states that Pharaoh will be left in the wilderness. This means he will find refuge and safety.
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:5 indicates that Pharaoh will be thrown into the wilderness without refuge, signifying judgment and abandonment.

questions.question: Ezekiel 29:14 mentions a base kingdom. This suggests that Egypt will be elevated and restored.
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:14 describes Egypt as a base kingdom, indicating a position of lowliness and humiliation, not elevation.

hard.title: Ezekiel Chapter 29 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Ezekiel Chapter 29.

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29:15, what will happen to the kingdom of Egypt after the captivity?
options: It shall be the basest of the kingdoms and shall no longer exalt itself above the nations
It shall become the greatest empire on earth
It shall rule over all nations forever
It shall be completely destroyed without restoration
questions.correctAnswer: It shall be the basest of the kingdoms and shall no longer exalt itself above the nations
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:15 states that Egypt 'shall be the basest of the kingdoms; neither shall it exalt itself any more above the nations.'

questions.question: What does Ezekiel 29:16 say will no longer be the confidence of the house of Israel?
options: Egypt, because it brings their iniquity to remembrance
questions.correctAnswer: Egypt, because it brings their iniquity to remembrance
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:16 states that Egypt 'shall be no more the confidence of the house of Israel, which bringeth their iniquity to remembrance.'

questions.question: In Ezekiel 29:18, what did Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon do to Tyrus?
options: Caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus, making every head bald and every shoulder peeled
Made a peaceful alliance with Tyrus
Built a wall around Tyrus for protection
questions.correctAnswer: Caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus, making every head bald and every shoulder peeled
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:18 describes how Nebuchadrezzar 'caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled.'

questions.question: What was Nebuchadrezzar's reward for serving against Tyrus according to Ezekiel 29:19?
options: The land of Egypt, including its multitude, spoil, and prey
A large sum of gold from Egypt
A diplomatic marriage alliance with Egypt
questions.correctAnswer: The land of Egypt, including its multitude, spoil, and prey
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:19 states, 'I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and take her prey.'

questions.question: According to Ezekiel 29:20, why was Egypt given to Nebuchadrezzar?
options: Because they wrought for God and Nebuchadrezzar served against Egypt
Because Egypt was peaceful and submitted willingly
Because Nebuchadrezzar paid a large tribute
Because Egypt had conquered Babylon previously
questions.correctAnswer: Because they wrought for God and Nebuchadrezzar served against Egypt
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:20 says, 'I have given him the land of Egypt for his labour wherewith he served against it, because they wrought for me, saith the Lord GOD.'

questions.question: What will happen to the horn of the house of Israel as stated in Ezekiel 29:21?
options: It will bud forth and give opening of the mouth in the midst of them
It will be broken and never restored
It will be hidden in the wilderness
It will be taken by Nebuchadrezzar
questions.correctAnswer: It will bud forth and give opening of the mouth in the midst of them
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:21 states, 'I will cause the horn of the house of Israel to bud forth, and I will give thee the opening of the mouth in the midst of them.'

questions.question: What does the Hebrew word 'qeren' (horn) in Ezekiel 29:21 mean?
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word 'qeren' (קֶרֶן) often symbolizes strength or power, as seen in Ezekiel 29:21 referring to the 'horn of the house of Israel.'

questions.question: Which literary device is primarily used in Ezekiel 29:4-5 where Egypt is called 'the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers'?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:3-5 uses a metaphor comparing Pharaoh to a 'great dragon' lying in the rivers, symbolizing Egypt's pride and power.

questions.question: Which Old Testament passage connects to Ezekiel 29:11's prophecy about Egypt being uninhabited for forty years?
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 25:11-12 speaks of seventy years of desolation for nations including Egypt, echoing Ezekiel 29:11's theme of desolation and captivity.

questions.question: Which New Testament passage can be seen as fulfilling the theme of God's sovereignty over nations found in Ezekiel 29:16?
questions.explanation: Acts 17:26 speaks of God determining the times and places of nations, connecting with Ezekiel 29:16's emphasis that Israel and the nations will know that God is Lord.

questions.question: What comes before Ezekiel 29:15, which states Egypt shall be 'the basest of the kingdoms'?
options: God promises to gather the Egyptians from the nations where they were scattered
questions.correctAnswer: God promises to gather the Egyptians from the nations where they were scattered
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:13-14 precedes verse 15 with God's promise to gather the Egyptians and bring them back, setting context for Egypt becoming a base kingdom.

questions.question: How does Ezekiel 29:6 use the imagery of a 'staff of reed' in relation to Egypt's role with Israel?
options: To symbolize Egypt as weak and easily broken when Israel leaned on it
To indicate Egypt as a strong support for Israel
To describe Egypt as a weapon against Israel
To depict Egypt as a pathway for Israel's journey
questions.correctAnswer: To symbolize Egypt as weak and easily broken when Israel leaned on it
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:6 describes Egypt as a 'staff of reed' that breaks when Israel leans on it, symbolizing unreliable support.

questions.question: What typology can be seen in Ezekiel 29:18-20 regarding Nebuchadrezzar's treatment of Egypt?
options: Nebuchadrezzar as God's instrument of judgment and reward
Tyrus as a symbol of Israel's faithfulness
questions.correctAnswer: Nebuchadrezzar as God's instrument of judgment and reward
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:18-20 portrays Nebuchadrezzar serving against Egypt as labor for God, who rewards him with Egypt's land, typifying divine judgment and recompense.

questions.question: How does Ezekiel 29:9-10 employ parallelism in describing Egypt's desolation?
options: By paralleling the land and rivers both becoming desolate and waste
By repeating the phrase 'I am the LORD' twice
questions.correctAnswer: By paralleling the land and rivers both becoming desolate and waste
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:9-10 uses parallelism by stating 'the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste' and 'I am against thee, and against thy rivers,' highlighting total desolation.

questions.question: True or False: According to Ezekiel 29:12, the Egyptians will be scattered among the nations and dispersed through the countries.
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:12 explicitly states God will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the countries.

theological.title: Ezekiel Chapter 29 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Ezekiel Chapter 29 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Ezekiel 29:6 teach about God's nature in relation to the people of Israel?
options: God is sovereign over nations and disciplines those who harm His people
God is indifferent to the suffering of Israel
God promises unconditional victory to Israel regardless of their faithfulness
God allows Egypt to remain unpunished despite their opposition
questions.correctAnswer: God is sovereign over nations and disciplines those who harm His people
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:6 states that all inhabitants of Egypt shall know that God is the LORD because Egypt was a staff of reed to Israel but broke when leaned upon, showing God's sovereign judgment over Egypt for its treatment of Israel.

questions.question: What doctrine regarding divine judgment and human pride is taught in Ezekiel 29:9?
options: God judges nations that arrogantly claim ownership over His creation
God rewards nations that claim rivers as their own
Human pride is irrelevant to divine plans
God's judgment is limited to Israel only
questions.correctAnswer: God judges nations that arrogantly claim ownership over His creation
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:9 shows God's judgment on Egypt because it said, 'The river is mine, and I have made it,' illustrating condemnation of human pride claiming divine sovereignty.

questions.question: What doctrine about God's justice and temporal punishment does Ezekiel 29:11 teach?
options: God imposes a defined period of desolation to fulfill His justice
God's punishments are eternal without restoration
God does not punish nations but only individuals
God's justice is capricious and unpredictable
questions.correctAnswer: God imposes a defined period of desolation to fulfill His justice
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:11 states that the land of Egypt shall be uninhabited for forty years, indicating a temporal and measured divine punishment.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Ezekiel 29:10 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:10 shows God's sovereign power in declaring He will make Egypt utterly waste and desolate, exercising control over nations and nature.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is highlighted in Ezekiel 29:21 when God promises to cause the horn of Israel to bud forth?
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:21 shows God's faithfulness in promising restoration and empowerment to Israel despite prior judgment.

questions.question: How does the judgment of Egypt in Ezekiel 29 prepare the theological theme of God’s judgment on Gentile powers found in Daniel?
options: It prefigures God’s sovereign control and judgment over Gentile kingdoms
It contrasts with Daniel where Gentile kingdoms are exalted
It denies any future restoration of Gentile nations
It primarily focuses on Israel’s internal failures
questions.correctAnswer: It prefigures God’s sovereign control and judgment over Gentile kingdoms
questions.explanation: The chapter’s judgment of Egypt anticipates themes in Daniel about God’s authority over Gentile empires, emphasizing divine sovereignty over worldly powers.

questions.question: In what way does Ezekiel 29:13-14 connect to the Babylonian exile and later restoration theology?
options: It foretells the eventual regathering of scattered nations by God
It denies any future restoration after exile
It predicts permanent destruction without hope
It focuses exclusively on Israel’s captivity
questions.correctAnswer: It foretells the eventual regathering of scattered nations by God
questions.explanation: Ezekiel 29:13-14 promises God will gather Egypt after 40 years, paralleling themes of exile and restoration in Israel’s history.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Ezekiel 29:3 and 29:9 teach about human arrogance and divine sovereignty?
options: Human claims of ownership over creation are futile against God’s sovereign judgment
Human sovereignty is equal to God’s
God rewards human pride as a sign of power
Divine sovereignty is limited by human power
questions.correctAnswer: Human claims of ownership over creation are futile against God’s sovereign judgment
questions.explanation: Verse 3 depicts Pharaoh as claiming the river as his own, while verse 9 shows God judging Egypt for this arrogance, teaching God’s ultimate sovereignty.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Ezekiel 29:11 and 29:12 teach about the nature and purpose of divine judgment?
options: Divine judgment is both punitive and disciplinary, allowing for eventual restoration
Divine judgment is eternal without hope
Judgment ignores the impact on nations
God’s judgment is random and unmeasured
questions.correctAnswer: Divine judgment is both punitive and disciplinary, allowing for eventual restoration
questions.explanation: Verse 11’s 40-year desolation and verse 12’s scattering indicate judgment with a defined period and purpose, not eternal destruction.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Ezekiel 29:18-20 teach about God’s use of foreign powers in His redemptive plan?
options: God sovereignly uses pagan kingdoms like Babylon to accomplish His purposes
God abandons His people to foreign powers without purpose
Foreign powers act independently of God's will
God’s plan excludes Gentile nations completely
questions.correctAnswer: God sovereignly uses pagan kingdoms like Babylon to accomplish His purposes
questions.explanation: Verses 18-20 show Babylon’s conquest of Egypt as serving God’s plan, affirming divine sovereignty over all nations, even pagan ones.

questions.question: Skeptics claim Ezekiel 29:11-12's 40 years of desolation is historically inaccurate and symbolic at best. What does the passage actually teach?
options: The 40 years refer to a definite period of judgment and exile with eventual restoration
The 40 years is purely symbolic with no real consequence
The passage promises permanent destruction without return
It denies that Egypt was ever punished
questions.correctAnswer: The 40 years refer to a definite period of judgment and exile with eventual restoration
questions.explanation: Verses 11-12 specify a 40-year desolation followed by regathering (verse 13), showing a measured judgment with restoration, not mere symbolism.

questions.question: What doctrine about the consequences of idolatry and false security is taught in Ezekiel 29:7?
options: Relying on false supports leads to ruin and brokenness
False security is rewarded by God
God ignores human reliance on idols
questions.correctAnswer: Relying on false supports leads to ruin and brokenness
questions.explanation: Verse 7 describes Egypt as a staff of reed that breaks when leaned upon, illustrating the futility of trusting in false sources rather than God.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is chiefly demonstrated in Ezekiel 29:15 where Egypt is said to be the basest of kingdoms?
questions.explanation: The designation of Egypt as the basest kingdom reflects God’s just punishment and diminution of a proud nation that opposed His people.

questions.question: How does Ezekiel 29:16’s teaching about Israel’s confidence relate to the doctrine of sanctification?
options: God removes false confidence in worldly powers to sanctify His people
Israel’s sin is ignored in sanctification
Confidence in Egypt remains the foundation of sanctification
questions.correctAnswer: God removes false confidence in worldly powers to sanctify His people
questions.explanation: Verse 16 states Egypt will no longer be Israel’s confidence, showing God’s sanctifying work in redirecting trust away from worldly powers to Himself.

questions.question: What theological implication does Ezekiel 29:4’s imagery of hooks and fish have regarding God’s control over nature and nations?
options: God exercises sovereign control over natural elements and political powers
Nature and nations operate independently from God
God’s power is limited to spiritual realms only
The imagery encourages human mastery over nature
questions.correctAnswer: God exercises sovereign control over natural elements and political powers
questions.explanation: Verse 4’s metaphor of hooks in Pharaoh’s jaws and fish sticking to scales symbolizes God’s sovereign restraint and control over Egypt and its environment.
